summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The protests that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, known as the Monsoon Revolution, mark the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who were previously visible now live in hiding. A Washington Blade assessment of 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, found Bangladesh's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The current national incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022, and the violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025; five unidentified individuals were accused.

The legal baseline sits under the Penal Code 1860, which criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment. The provision is rarely prosecuted but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Bangladesh, issued September 2023 and updated April 2026, records that the scope of Section 377 remains ambiguous, including uncertainty over whether it reaches female-female conduct. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017) compiled Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues, citing fact-finding missions and the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.

Against that framework, Bangladesh has formally recognised third-gender identity since 2013, with hijra recognised as a legal third gender and gender-marker change permitted since 2014, and hijra and LGBTIQ pride events have been held. A rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021. Formal recognition has not prevented the practical rollback documented since 2024.

Police conduct toward visibly trans people is a distinct exposure. After hijras refused police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates in Narayanganj, a traditional livelihood. In April 2024, five trans women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to roughly a month in custody, which places policing of visibly trans people at the country's principal international transit hub.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern is extortion-driven rather than prosecution-driven: police harass people presumed LGBTIQ under a statute they seldom take to trial, and the 2025 incidents in Gomdondi Phultala and Narayanganj followed refusals to pay rather than any alleged offence. A visitor who reads as visibly trans should expect demand-side encounters with officers more than court proceedings.

Bangladesh's recognition of hijra as third gender since 2013 and 2014, and the election of a trans woman mayor in 2021, place the country ahead of most regional neighbours on paper. The divergence between that formal status and the post-2024 security environment is the central caution for anyone relying on statutory rights when assessing risk.

Geographic spread matters: the 2025 homicide occurred in the hill district of Rangamati, the extortion violence in Khulna and Narayanganj divisions, the arrest of street-collecting hijras in Narayanganj, and the transit-hub arrests in Dhaka. No single city or region is documented as safe, and the JMBF 2025 figures are national rather than metropolitan.
localsOnly:
Hijra communities sustain themselves in part through traditional street livelihoods, including collecting money from vehicles and begging, and both practices have drawn arrest and police retaliation. The twelve hijras arrested in Narayanganj on 17 September 2025 were engaged in the former; the five trans women arrested near Dhaka's international airport in April 2024 were engaged in the latter.

Activists who were publicly visible before August 2024 have changed behaviour substantially. The trans advocate featured in reporting on the post-revolution period now lives in hiding, and organised LGBTIQ and hijra visibility has contracted even where pride events had previously been held.

Domestic advocacy continues through organisations such as JMBF, which produces the annual violation counts cited above, and through legal channels including the third-gender recognition framework and gender-marker change.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve the practical requirements or turnaround for a foreign visitor seeking any gender-marker or documentation alignment in Bangladesh, nor whether entry screening by immigration or customs officers involves questions capable of outing a trans traveller. No source documents visa or border rules with reference to gender identity.

Section 377's application to female-female conduct remains unsettled in the cited material, with the UK Home Office noting the ambiguity and ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report reaching different readings in different passages. The treatment of trans-masculine visitors specifically is not addressed by any source here; nearly all documented violence concerns hijra and trans women.

No source in this inventory documents current conditions for gender-affirming healthcare access, its availability to non-residents, or any legal status for same-sex marriage or foreign partner recognition. The current composition and policy direction of the caretaker government installed after August 2024 is not described beyond the security assessments cited.
